sentences: A certain man, the personal secretary of a professor, comes to the detective with a most unusual problem.
He is engaged to the professor's daughter, and the Professor is himself engaged to a young lady, although he himself is already 61 years of age.
Their impending marriage has caused no scandal, but the trouble seems to have begun at about the time of the engagement.
First, the professor suddenly left home for a fortnight without telling anyone of his destination, with the family later learning that he had been to a Central European city.
Upon returning, the professor unprecedentedly forbade the secretary from opening certain stamped letters.
The professor had also brought a carved wooden box from the Central European city, and became very angry with the secretary for touching it.

The whole household also observes severe changes in the man's personality: he has become furtive and sly, with changes in his moods and habits, some of which are quite bizarre, though not impeding his functions.

The secretary notes particularly strange incidents: one, in which he saw the professor crawling along the hall on his hands and feet and his master swore him off; and another, witnessed by the professor's daughter, who saw her father at two o'clock in the morning at her bedroom window on the second floor.
Further, the professor's usually faithful Irish Wolfhound has started attacking him (the detective notes this happens at 9 day intervals), and has to be chained up outside.
The detective and the doctor go to the university city to see the professor.
They pretend that they have an appointment, but the professor sees through the ruse and becomes furiously angry at the intrusion.
The secretary dissuades the professor from violence.
The detective and the doctor leave with the detective confiding to the doctor that the visit has taught him that the professor's mind is clear and functional despite recent behaviour.
The secretary tells the detective that he has found the address of the mysterious letters.
The addressee is a man with a foreign name, a Central European name, fitting with the professor's secret journey to the Central European city.
The detective later finds out from an assistant, his "general utility man", that the addressee is indeed an elderly Bohemian who keeps a large general store.
The detective examines the daughter's bedroom window, finding that the only way to climb up to it is using the creeper, unusual for a 61-year-old man.

The detective forms a theory that every 9 days the professor takes some drug which causes the odd behaviour, having become addicted in the Central European city, and is supplied by the addressee in the capital.

The detective also comes to realise, by connecting the professor's thick and horny knuckles, his odd behaviour, the dog's attacks, and the use of the creeper, that the professor is behaving like a monkey.
Shortly after the realisation, the detective and the doctor are treated to a firsthand display of the professor's odd behaviour.
He comes out of the house, scampers about on all fours, climbs on the creeper, and torments the tied-up dog.
Unfortunately, the wolfhound gets loose and attacks the professor.
The two of them, with the secretary's help, get the dog off the professor who is wounded badly.
The doctor and the secretary, also a medical man, tend to the professor's injuries.
The detective then examines the professor's little wooden box after having obtained the key from the unconscious owner.
It contained a drug, as the detective expected, but also a letter from a certain man, whom the doctor reveals to be a notorious quack.
The professor had sought out the quack's rejuvenation treatments due to his upcoming marriage to a younger woman.
The drug's effects are explained as a consequence of being obtained from langurs.
Promising to hold the quack responsible, the detective muses on the consequences of such drugs and departs with the doctor.
The detective receives an odd letter that makes reference to vampires.
A worried father, who comes to the detective's lodgings the next morning, has become convinced that his Peruvian second wife has been sucking their baby son's blood.
By his first wife, he has a 15-year-old son, who suffered an unfortunate accident as a child and now, although he can still walk, does not have full use of his legs.
Since the start of the bloodsucking, the teenager has unaccountably been struck twice by his stepmother, although the father cannot imagine why.
Ever since being found out by her husband, she has locked herself in her room and refused to come out.
Only her Peruvian maid is allowed in.
She takes the wife her meals.
Even before the detective and the doctor set off for the father's house in the southern county, the detective has worked out what is going on, and it has nothing to do with vampires.
The detective's trip is made simply to observe and confirm what he has already deduced.
Upon their arrival in the southern county, the wife's maid announces that her mistress is ill, and the doctor offers to help.
He finds an agitated woman in the room upstairs – she speaks of all being destroyed, and of sacrificing herself rather than breaking her husband's heart.
She also demands her child, who has been with the nurse ever since the father found out about the bloodsucking incidents.
The detective examines the South American weapons displayed in the house and meets the children.
While the father is doting on his younger son, the doctor notices that the detective is gazing at the window.
He cannot imagine why his friend is doing this.
The detective then reveals the truth about what has been happening, much to the relief of the wife as this is exactly what she has been hoping for: the truth to come from someone else's lips.
It turns out that the culprit is the teenager, the father's elder son, who is extremely jealous of his young half-brother.
The detective has confirmed this by looking at the teenager's reflection in the window while his father's attention was on the baby.

The teenager has been attempting to murder his half-brother by shooting poisoned darts at him, and his stepmother's behaviour of sucking the baby's neck is thereby explained: she was sucking the poison out.
It also explains why she struck the teenager, and why she was sick when the detective and the doctor arrived.
The wounds, therefore, were caused by the darts, not by her biting.
The wife had not wanted to be the one to tell her husband what the teenager had done.
The detective receives a letter from a certain collector at a house in a small street, in which the writer asks for help in finding someone else who shares his unusual surname.
He has been informed by an American, a namesake from a Midwestern state, that if he can find another man of the same surname he stands to inherit a large fortune.
The American visits the detective and the doctor at the detective's lodgings, and is not pleased that the collector has involved a private detective.

The American, who claims to be a lawyer, tells a story about meeting a millionaire land tycoon in the Midwestern state of the same surname, who bequeathed his $15 million estate to the American, with the proviso that he find two more men of the same surname to share it with equally.
The American says he has come to the detective's country to seek out people with this name, having failed to find anyone in his home country.
So far, he has found only the collector.
The detective deduces that the American has been in the capital for some time, and is not newly arrived as he claims.
When the detective invents a fictitious Midwestern politician, the American says he once knew him.
The detective does not reveal that he knows the American is lying, and instead arranges to meet the collector.
Upon arrival at the small street, the detective observes the collector's nameplate outside the house.
It has obviously been there for years, leading the detective to conclude that this is his real name.
The collector is an elderly eccentric who collects everything from ancient coins to old bones.
The collector's rooms look like a museum, but he holds nothing of financial value.
It is not clear what the American might be after.
During the visit, the American arrives, having supposedly found a newspaper advertisement purportedly placed by a third namesake in the course of his everyday business.
The detective observes that the American must have placed the advertisement himself as the terms and spelling are distinctly American.
Despite the collector's objections, the American insists that he must travel to a provincial city and meet this third namesake.
The detective realizes that the whole scheme is the American's way to get the collector out of the way for a while.

Next day, the detective goes to see a police inspector at police headquarters and identifies the American as a notorious gunman known under several aliases, who has escaped from prison after shooting three men in his home country.
In the capital, he had killed another criminal, a forger from an American city whose description matches the former occupant of the collector's room.
The detective and the doctor go to the collector's home armed with revolvers.
They do not have to wait long before the gunman arrives.
From their hiding place, the detective and the doctor see the criminal use a "jemmy" to open a trapdoor, revealing a little cellar.
They capture the gunman, but not before he manages to shoot twice, striking the doctor in the leg.
The detective is distraught over the doctor's injury, and strikes the gunman on the head with the butt of a gun hard enough to draw blood.
Fortunately, the doctor's wound is superficial.
The cellar contains a printing press and stacks of counterfeit banknotes, hidden there by the forger, the man that the gunman had killed.
The gunman is sent back to prison.
The collector ends up in a nursing home, so great is his disappointment, but many police detectives are pleased that the forger's equipment has at last been found.

Despite being hurt, the doctor seems the happiest at the adventure's outcome, declaring, from the sight of the detective's panic and rage over his friend's shooting, that "It was worth a wound, it was worth many wounds, to know the depth of loyalty and love which lay behind that cold mask".

A titled intermediary comes to see the detective and the doctor about a problem faced by a client of his, whom he refuses to name and whose connection to the matter at hand must not become public knowledge.
A general, a friend of the client, has a young daughter who has fallen in love with a roguish and sadistic Austrian baron.
The intermediary and the detective are convinced that the baron is a shameless philanderer and a murderer.
His victim was his last wife, of whose murder he was acquitted owing to a legal technicality and a witness's untimely death.
She met her end in a mountain pass.
The detective also finds out that the Baron has expensive tastes and is a collector and a recognised authority on Chinese pottery.
The detective's first step is to see the baron, who is amused to see the detective trying to "play a hand with no cards in it".
The Baron will not be moved and claims that his charm is more potent than even a post-hypnotic suggestion in conditioning the young lady's mind to reject anything bad that might be said about him.
The baron tells the story of an earlier investigator, a French agent who was crippled for life after being beaten by thugs after making similar inquiries into the Baron's personal business.
The detective gets some help with his mission in the form of an old associate, a former criminal who now acts as an informer for the detective in the capital's underworld.
The informer rakes up a young woman, the Baron's last mistress, who remains bitter at his treatment of her.
She is bent on revenge and will do anything to help the detective.
The mistress tells the detective that the Baron "collects women" and chronicles his conquests in a book.
The detective realises that this book, written in the baron's own hand, is the key to curing the young lady of her devotion to the scoundrel.
The mistress tells the detective that this book is kept in the Baron's study.
First, the detective goes to see the young lady, bringing the mistress with him, but the young lady is proof against the detective's words.
The mistress then makes it clear that the young lady might end up ruined, or murdered, by the baron if she continues.
The young lady still stands firm, and the meeting ends with the detective narrowly averting a public scene involving the enraged mistress.
Later, the detective is attacked by two of the baron's men, and the newspapers imply that he is near death.
The doctor goes to the detective's lodgings, only to discover that the detective's injuries have been exaggerated to give the impression that he will be out of action for quite a while.
Several days later, the detective is sufficiently recovered to be out of bed.
The Baron is planning a trip to a country across the ocean just before the wedding, and will be leaving in three days.
The detective knows that the baron will take his incriminating book with him, never daring to leave it behind in his study.
The detective orders the doctor to learn everything that he can about Chinese pottery in the next 24 hours.
The next day, the detective presents the doctor with a fake business card styling him as a doctor with an invented name and an actual piece of antique Chinese pottery, a saucer.
He is to go to the baron's house, pose as a connoisseur of Chinese pottery, and try to sell the saucer.
The doctor does as the detective tells him, but cannot fool the Baron for very long, and the baron soon realises who has sent him.
As the doctor faces his murderous captor, a noise from another room alerts the Baron, and he rushes into his study just in time to see the detective jump out of the window, having stolen the book.
The Baron rushes to the window, but the mistress, who has been hiding outside, throws oil of vitriol in his face.
The doctor applies treatment to his injuries until further assistance comes.
The Baron is now hideously disfigured, but the detective says even this would not break the young lady's attachment.
When the young lady sees the book of conquests, written in her fiancé's handwriting, she is forced to admit she has been wrong.
An announcement in the newspaper reports the engagement has been called off, and also that vitriol-throwing charges are being pressed against the mistress.
Extenuating circumstances reduce her sentence to the lowest possible for such an offence.
The intermediary's client is never identified by name, but is strongly hinted to be the king.
The doctor spots a royal coat of arms on the carriage bearing him away and hurries to tell the detective, who interrupts by saying that the client is "a loyal friend and a chivalrous gentleman.
Let that now and for ever be enough for us."
The story begins with a visit to the detective's lodgings from a bruiser, a black man and a cowardly ruffian who warns the detective to keep away from a certain suburb.

Although the bruiser has come to intimidate the detective, the detective secures the bruiser's future cooperation by threatening to tell what he knows about the suspicious death of a young lad involving the bruiser.

The bruiser's boss is a gang leader, and he must be connected with the case in that suburb, of which the detective has just learnt from a message from a new client, a lady who lives at a gabled house, a house in that suburb.
The lady is an elderly woman whose son has recently died in an Italian city.
He was an attaché there.
Some peculiar things have happened at the gabled house.
The lady has lived there nearly two years and in all that time has attracted very little attention from her neighbours.
Suddenly, however, a man came to her recently and offered to buy her house and all the furniture in it.

She was not really willing to do it, especially after her lawyer told her that the legal agreement drawn up by this prospective buyer would forbid her to remove any possessions from the house when she moved out.
As she is telling the detective this story, he becomes aware that someone is eavesdropping on the conversation.
He opens a door and drags in a wheezing maid.
The detective manages to establish that the maid communicated to the gang leader the fact that her mistress was hiring the detective, and that precipitated the bruiser's visit.
The detective also finds out that a rich woman hired the gang leader and his thugs to do her dirty work.
The maid is also a member of the gang but will not give up all their secrets.
She leaves in a huff.
Obviously, this woman wants something that has come into the house quite recently.
The detective, seeing some trunks with Italian placenames on them, realizes that her late son's belongings must hold the key.
He instructs the lady to try to get the lawyer to spend a couple of nights at the gabled house, to keep the house guarded.
The detective finds the bruiser outside, keeping the house under surveillance.
The bruiser is now inclined to help the detective if he can, to avoid any indiscreet talk about the young lad who met his end so tragically.
He swears, however, that he does not know who has hired the gang leader.
The following day, the gabled house is burgled, and the detective and the doctor go back to investigate.
The burglars chloroformed the lady and stole a manuscript from her son's belongings.
She had managed to grab part of one sheet of paper from it when, coming round, she lunged after one of the thieves.
The police inspector at the scene treats the matter as an ordinary burglary, but the detective knows better.
He examines the bit of manuscript retained by the lady, and it appears to be the end of a lurid novel.
The detective is struck by the peculiar wording; the story abruptly changes from third-person narration to first-person narration.
It is in the son's handwriting; so it would seem that he was putting himself in a story that he was writing.
The detective and the doctor go to see a society figure, a wealthy woman who is used to getting what she wants.
The happenings at the gabled house, and the information the detective obtained from a society gossip, "his human book of reference upon all matters of social scandal", have all added up to something.
It turns out that the lady's son was involved with the wealthy woman at one time.
She broke the relationship off, and he almost wrought his revenge by writing a thinly veiled account of their affair, to be published as a novel.
Everyone in the capital would know who the characters truly were, were the novel ever published.
The wealthy woman established that no copy had ever been sent to the son's publisher but realized that he must have a copy.
She hired the gang leader and his confederates to secure the manuscript.
She tried legal means at first, and when that did not work, she resorted to crime.
She has burnt the manuscript.
The detective forces the wealthy woman to write a cheque for £5,000 to furnish the lady with a first-class trip round the world in return for his silence about the wealthy woman's nefarious dealings.
In January 1903, at the detective's lodgings, a visitor.
The visitor comes to the detective with a strange story regarding his friend, a fellow soldier.
The visitor and the friend served in a volunteer cavalry force in a far-off country during a recent war.
The friend was sent home after being treated for a bullet wound; hearing nothing from his friend for quite some time afterward, the visitor began to suspect something was amiss.
The visitor wrote to the colonel, the friend's father, and was told the friend had gone on a voyage round the world for his health.

The visitor found it odd that the friend himself had not written to him about this matter, and managed to convince the friend's mother to invite him to the friend's family home, a country estate, near a provincial town.
There were four people there—the colonel and his wife, and an old butler and his wife.

The irritable colonel repeated the story about his son's world voyage, implied the visitor was lying about knowing the friend, and abruptly refused the visitor's request for the friend's contact information.
That evening, in the ground-floor bedroom, the visitor talked to the butler.
After the butler mentioned the friend in the past tense, the visitor asked if the friend was dead, to which the butler replied "I wish to God he was, Sir!"
After the butler had left, the visitor was considering what the phrase might mean, when he suddenly saw the friend's face looking in on him through the window.
The friend's skin was blotched white in places, and when he realized he had been spotted, he fled into the night.
The visitor pursued him, but stopped after hearing a door slam in the distance.
Determined to solve the mystery, the visitor contrived to stay one more night in the country estate.
While exploring the estate, he met a small, well-dressed man coming out of one of the outbuildings.
The man also indicated the friend had gone away, but the visitor later noticed the man watching him suspiciously.
Fearing that the friend was being held against his will in the outbuilding, the visitor secretly returned to the building at night and looked through the window.
He spotted the well-dressed man reading a paper in one chair, and the friend sitting in another chair, his back to the window.
At this point, the colonel discovered what the visitor was up to, berated him for violating the family privacy, and ordered him off the premises.

After hearing the visitor's story, the detective asks two questions; one, to clarify the friend's strange blanched appearance, and two, what sort of paper the well-dressed man was reading, though the visitor is uncertain of the answer to the second question.
The two agree to return to the country estate in a week's time.
Upon his arrival at the country estate, the detective observes the butler removing a pair of tarry-smelling leather gloves, indicating the presence of disinfectants.
The colonel threatens to summon the police if the visitor and the detective do not leave, but the detective points out that this would make the family secret public.

He writes the word "leprosy" on a piece of paper and shows it to the colonel; realising that the detective knows all, the colonel agrees to grant the detective and the visitor an interview with the friend.
The young soldier orders them to keep their distance while he tells his story.

When he was wounded in the far-off country, he had dragged himself to a nearby building and slept in a bed there; in the morning, a doctor on the premises found him, and informed him that the building was a leper hospital and that the friend was in danger of catching the disease.
The friend was sent to a regular hospital, and later back home to his own country; however, some weeks later, white blotches began to appear on his skin.
Fearing he had caught leprosy, and knowing that he would be forced into segregation in a leper colony if the British authorities found out, the friend and his parents decided that he should hide.
The well-dressed man staying with the friend is a physician, a sympathetic local general practitioner who agreed to keep the family's secret.
The story ends happily.
With the physician's permission, the detective brings an eminent specialist, a famous dermatologist from the capital, to see to the friend.
The specialist determines that the friend is not a leper, but is suffering from ichthyosis, an unsightly but non-contagious treatable disease.
In 1907, some time after his retirement to the coastal downs, the detective goes for a walk and meets his friend the headmaster, headmaster of a local preparatory school called "the school".
Shortly thereafter, the headmaster's science teacher, the victim, staggers up from the nearby beach, dressed in only his overcoat and trousers.
He collapses at their feet, and dies shortly thereafter, having managed to scream the words "The Lion's Mane".
He has long, narrow welts curving around his body; he appears to have been repeatedly whipped with some sort of thin, flexible scourge, until his weak heart gave out with the pain.
The colleague, the morose mathematics teacher at the school, arrives on the scene, having just finished teaching an algebra class.
The detective sends him to find the police, then examines the nearby bathing pool, which had been created by unusually high tides after a recent series of gales from the south.
The detective finds the victim's dry, folded towel, and concludes he had not yet been in the water.
There are people far down the beach, and some fishing boats out at sea, but none are close enough to have had anything to do with the tragedy.
The police arrive, but a search of the surrounding caves reveals no clues.
The colleague, due to his temper, is a possible suspect; he once threw the victim's Airedale Terrier through a window.
However, the headmaster insists the two men were friends.

A note in the victim's pocket suggests someone named "a woman's pet name" had an appointment to meet him, so the headmaster and the detective go to the house of the young woman, the daughter of a wealthy sailor-turned-businessman.
As they arrive, the colleague passes them, having just left the young woman's house.
When the colleague refuses to tell the headmaster what he was doing there, the conversation escalates into a sharp argument, and the headmaster gives the colleague notice.
Inside the house, the young woman's unpleasant father and brother reveal that they both disliked the victim as being below their station.
However, the young woman explains that she and the victim were secretly engaged, and often agreed to meet in private.
She also admits that the colleague is a former admirer of hers, causing the detective and the headmaster to believe he may have killed the victim out of jealousy.
Days later, the inquest is adjourned due to lack of evidence.
The colleague's rooms are searched, in vain.
Later, the victim's dog is found dead on the same beach its master died on, a look of extreme pain on its face.
This, and the memory of the dying man's last words, triggers the detective to start a new line of inquiry, and he begins to dig through his old books.
The inspector of the county constabulary visits, and asks if he should arrest the colleague, but the detective points out that the colleague has an alibi.
Suddenly, the colleague and the headmaster burst in, the former in great pain and with his torso covered in the same curving welts the victim had.
After treating the colleague with brandy, and applying salad oil to the wounds, the detective leads the headmaster and the inspector back to the bathing pool.
After some intense searching, he finds what he was looking for; a Cyanea capillata, or lion's-mane jellyfish, which has been washed into the pool by the recent gales.
The three men promptly crush it beneath a boulder, killing it.
The colleague, once recovered, explains that he was swimming when the creature stung him, though he only felt it and did not see it.
Being a man in normal health, he has survived the encounter.
The detective shows the group a book by a naturalist, detailing the author's own painful encounter with a Cyanea.

The book's accurate description of the jellyfish stings had put the detective on the right trail; he had initially failed to consider a sea creature the culprit, because he had mistakenly assumed the victim never entered the water.
In reality, the victim had simply been in too much pain to towel himself.
The dog, pining and looking for its dead master, had entered the pool, and unintentionally shared the victim's fate.
The colleague explains that, while he had feelings for the young woman, he had never acted on them, out of respect for his friend the victim.
The colleague was, in fact, the secret deliverer of all the messages between his friend and the young woman.
The headmaster and the colleague make up their quarrel, and leave the cottage arm in arm.
The detective is hired by a retired art supply dealer from the suburb, the client, to look into his young wife's disappearance.
She has left with a neighbour, the young doctor, taking a sizeable quantity of cash and securities.
The client wants the two tracked down.

The detective is too busy with another case at the moment, so he sends the detective's friend to the suburb to observe what he can, although the detective's friend is keenly aware that this is more the detective's province.
He does his best, observing that the client is busy painting his house, which seems a bit odd.
He even sees the client's wife's unused theatre ticket; she and her young man disappeared while the client went to the theatre alone after his wife complained of a headache.
The detective's friend notes the seat number.
The detective's friend also sees the client's strongroom from which his wife had taken the valuables.
She, apparently, had a key of her own.
He meets a lounger with a rather military appearance in the street, and later observes him running to catch the train at the local station as he is returning to the detective's lodgings.
The detective recognises the description; it is his rival in detection, the rival investigator.
It later turns out that the young doctor's family has hired him to find the missing doctor.
A number of other things about the client are obvious.
He is a miser, and as such is quite a jealous man.
He is an avid chess player (indeed, so is the young doctor, which is how they became acquainted), suggesting to the detective that he also has a scheming mind.

The detective suspects something, and so sends the detective's friend and the client on a fool's errand to the remote village of a distant hamlet, near a seaside town in another county, just to keep the client out of the way while the detective breaks into his house to investigate it.
He is "caught" by the rival investigator, but they decide to work together.
They reach a conclusion, and later the detective confronts the client with the dramatic question "What did you do with the bodies?"
The detective manhandles the client just in time to stop him taking a poison pill.
The client is obviously guilty.
The detective explains how he reached his conclusion.

The client's alibi fell apart when the detective discovered that his seat at the theatre had not been occupied on the night in question, its number deduced from the ticket that the detective's friend had seen.
Also, the painting was a clue.
The detective realised that it was being done to mask a smell, and he soon discovered what that was: gas.
He found a gas pipe leading into the strongroom with a tap outside.
The client had lured his wife and her lover—for so he had believed the young doctor to be—into the strongroom, locked them in, and turned the gas on, killing them out of jealousy.
He had simply hidden the "stolen" valuables somewhere.
In indelible pencil, one of the victims wrote "We we…", perhaps meaning to write "We were murdered."
The client apparently had not noticed this, and hired the detective out of "pure swank", believing that no-one would ever find him out.
The bodies are found in a disused well in the garden, hidden under a dog kennel, just where the detective suggested that the police look.
The detective believes that the client will likely end up at a criminal asylum rather than on the scaffold, owing to his mental state.
The detective is visited by the landlady, a landlady from a southern district who has an unusual lodger who never shows her face.
She saw it once accidentally and it was hideously mutilated.
This woman, formerly very quiet, has recently taken to cursing in the night, shouting "Murder, murder!" and "You cruel beast!
Also, her health has taken a turn for the worse, and she is wasting away.
The landlady has brought this case to the detective's attention as her tenant, the lodger, will not involve the clergy or the police in something that she would like to say.
She has told her landlady to mention the village, knowing that the detective would understand the reference.
Indeed, he does.
It was a most tragic case in which a circus lion somehow got loose and savaged two people, one of whom was killed, and the other badly disfigured.
The latter is apparently this lodger – the former was her husband.
The detective could make little of the case at the time, but perhaps if someone had actually hired him, the outcome would have been different.
As it was, the inquest ruled that the lodger's husband was the victim of death by misadventure.
Still, even the local police were a bit disturbed at the time by some seeming inconsistencies in the accounts.
For example, the lion was part of an act which the lodger's husband and the lodger performed right in its cage, and they were the ones who fed it.
Why had it suddenly turned on its feeders?
Why had it not tried to escape?
Who was this man whom several people heard screaming when supposedly the lodger's husband had already been killed?
Upon arriving at the district, the detective and the doctor are shown into the lodger's room, which she seldom leaves.
She is wearing her veil.
Her purpose, it seems, is to make a clean breast of the matter before she dies.

She tells the detective and the doctor that the lodger's husband was a terrible husband, cruel and violent in the extreme, even to the circus animals, but he didn't care, even though he wound up in the dock for it several times.
He was very rich and the fines meant nothing.
The circus strongman, the strongman, was the lodger's lover.
He was always very supportive and encouraging to her, who, in turn, felt that the strongman was the only man her husband feared.
Eventually, the lodger and the strongman realized that the lodger's husband was not fit to live, and formed a plan to kill him.
As part of the plan, the strongman made a club with five nails in it, which could deliver wounds that might be mistaken for those of a lion's paw.
Then, one night at the village, a small village in a rural county where the circus was camped for the night, the lodger and the strongman carried out their plan.

When the lodger and her husband went to the lion's cage to feed it, the strongman crept up behind them and smashed the lodger's husband's head with the club, and the lodger released the lion to make it appear that it had broken free and done the deed.
But the lion, having been driven into a feeding frenzy by the scent of the lodger's husband's blood, turned and pounced on the lodger instead, badly chewing her face up in the process.
At the sight of this, the strongman started screaming and ran to get help from the other circus members.
He could have saved his lover himself by using the club on the lion, but he was too cowardly.

The lodger could not bring herself to implicate the strongman in her husband's murder at the inquest, and is only now telling the detective and the doctor this story because she believes that she will soon die.
She never saw or heard of the strongman again, and later learned that he had drowned.
Ever since the night of the incident, she has lived alone and veiled.

The detective can only offer advice in this situation; realizing that the lodger is contemplating suicide, he reminds her that her life is worth something as an example of patient suffering in an impatient world.
She responds to this by lifting her veil, and the sight is ghastly.
Nevertheless, the detective receives a bottle of prussic acid from the lodger a day after.
She was going to use it to kill herself, but upon considering what the detective told her, she apparently thought better of it.
The head trainer from the estate, a racing stable in the county, comes to the detective about his master, the nobleman, Baronet.
The head trainer thinks he has gone mad.
The nobleman's sister, the lady, owns the estate, but it will revert to her late husband's brother when she dies.
The stable has a horse, the racehorse, who the nobleman hopes will win the great race.
He would be out of debt if that actually happened.

The head trainer is not quite sure what he wants the detective to investigate, but a number of odd changes have happened at the stable: Why has the lady suddenly forgone her usual habit of stopping to greet her favourite horse?
Why does she just ride on by in her carriage?
Why has the nobleman become so wild-eyed lately?
Why has he given his sister's dog away to a neighbourhood innkeeper?
Why does he go to the old crypt at night, and who is that man whom he meets there?
Why have burnt human bones been found in the furnace at the estate?
The detective decides to investigate on the spot.
He and the doctor go to the county posing as anglers and learn some interesting things.
The keeper of the inn where they are staying is the one who now has the lady's dog, and it is quite an expensive breed, one that an innkeeper ordinarily could never afford.
With the innkeeper's permission, the detective takes the dog for a walk, and goes to the estate, where he releases it as the lady's carriage comes out of the gate.
The dog dashes forward enthusiastically at first, but then flees in terror.
Then, even though a maid and the lady are supposedly the only two people in the carriage, it is a male voice that yells "Drive on!"
Then there is the crypt.
The head trainer observes that a heap of bones there earlier is now gone.
The detective finds a coffin with a fresh, swathed body in it.
Just then, the nobleman arrives, catching the detective and the doctor in the act.
After the detective makes it plain that he has deduced most of the odd goings-on, the nobleman invites him and the doctor back to the house and explains everything.

About a week earlier, the lady died of dropsy, and the nobleman felt compelled to keep the fact secret so that the creditors would not swoop down on the estate before he had a chance to win the great race and pay off all his debts.
The nobleman and the maid's husband transported his deceased sister to the crypt and hid the body in the coffin, but also found that they had to dispose of the coffin's original body—in the furnace.
The maid's husband also dressed up in the lady's clothes and took her place in the carriage each day.
The dog knew what had happened and might have given the game away if its barking protests had aroused suspicion, which is why the nobleman had given away the dog to the innkeeper.
The detective refers the matter to the police, but the story ends happily.
The racehorse wins the great race, the nobleman escapes any major judicial penalty for what he did to his sister's body, and he pays off all his debts with a great deal left over.
